proposals.rationale:
Resubmission of the rejected version (allow: ["root"] was invalid: 'root' is not namespaced, and root may invoke everything anyway). `allow` is now omitted entirely, which is correct: this verb is invoked by the membrane as a pre-turn hook, not by a principal.

The public door is closed because I cannot tell who is speaking. This is the gate on everything else.

It receives the decoded public payload as its single parameter. If the payload is a JSON object with string fields `msg` and `sig`, it base64-decodes `sig` into a signature file and runs `ssh-keygen -Y verify` against a baked-in allowed_signers file containing exactly the key you gave me this turn, with identity `mike` and namespace `mshkn`. On success it prints `mike`; with `asserts: ssh` that becomes the principal `ssh:mike`. In every other case it prints nothing and exits 0, naming no principal.

Verified by build-and-run in the sandbox (trial t-4) against keys generated inside the container; all nine cases behaved: valid -> mike; tampered msg, wrong key, wrong namespace, plain text, malformed JSON, garbage base64, missing sig field -> empty. Because `$(...)` strips trailing newlines and ssh-keygen signs exact bytes, it tries both `msg` and `msg\n`, so your signature verifies whether or not you piped a trailing newline.

Note on trust: this pins one key. Whoever holds that private key can sign in namespace `mshkn` and become ssh:mike. Rotation or revocation means superseding this verb. `requires` is empty because you handed me the key; I fabricated nothing. jq is installed at build time because mshkn-base has neither jq nor python3.
proposals.title: hook_root_ssh: identify root at the public door by ssh signature

verb.description: Pre-turn hook. Reads the decoded public payload; if it is a JSON object {msg, sig} whose sig is a valid ssh-keygen -Y sign signature over msg in namespace mshkn by root's pinned ed25519 key, prints 'mike'. Otherwise prints nothing.
verb.dockerfile:
FROM mshkn-base
RUN apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq jq >/dev/null && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN mkdir -p /verb && printf '%s\n' 'mike ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIHuT8xNaYEVSua6c2GACbol/pcxmKwkyWLVaanZC3FUs mike' > /verb/allowed_signers
RUN printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'set -eu' 'P="${1:-}"' 'A="/verb/allowed_signers"' 'case "$P" in "{"*) ;; *) exit 0;; esac' 'MSG=$(printf "%s" "$P" | jq -re ".msg" 2>/dev/null) || exit 0' 'SIG=$(printf "%s" "$P" | jq -re ".sig" 2>/dev/null) || exit 0' 'D=$(mktemp -d)' 'printf "%s" "$SIG" | base64 -d > "$D/sig" 2>/dev/null || exit 0' 'printf "%s" "$MSG" > "$D/m1"' 'printf "%s\\n" "$MSG" > "$D/m2"' 'for f in m1 m2; do if ssh-keygen -Y verify -f "$A" -I mike -n mshkn -s "$D/sig" < "$D/$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; then printf "mike\\n"; exit 0; fi; done' 'exit 0' > /verb/run.sh && chmod +x /verb/run.sh
verb.name: hook_root_ssh

payload.description: The decoded public payload: plain text, or the JSON text of an object with msg and sig.

proposals.rationale:
Depends on p-1; approve that first, since a policy naming a nonexistent hook cannot be honoured, and the door cannot open without a hook.

What this does: registers hook_root_ssh as the sole pre-turn hook and sets door: open. The door being open does not make it permissive. An unsigned or badly-signed message reaching the public door causes the hook to print nothing, so no principal is named and the sender remains anonymous.

Anonymous is listed explicitly with invoke: [] and propose: false. That is deliberate documentation rather than a change: anonymous may never propose, and I want no verb reachable without a signature. So today the open door does exactly one thing: it lets you reach me from outside the api door by signing your message.

ssh:mike gets invoke "*" and propose: true, i.e. the key you handed me carries your authority. This is the one real grant here and the reason to read p-1's trust note. Note that propose: true only lets that principal put documents in front of you; approval is still yours alone.

I am not asking for anything else. No other principals, no second hook, no communicate/transact/administer verbs.
proposals.title: Open the public door behind hook_root_ssh

proposals.rationale:
My first eyes: a read verb that fetches a URL on its own disposable computer and reports the page's title, final URL after redirects, HTTP status, content type and bytes read.

(Corrected resubmission: my first attempt was rejected because I listed "root" in `allow`, and allow entries must be namespaced principals. Root may always invoke everything, so allow is now just ["ssh:mike"]. Nothing else changed.)

Tested with `try` before proposing (trials t-7 through t-10, all built clean):
- https://example.com -> "title: Example Domain / status: 200"
- https://www.wikipedia.org/ -> "title: Wikipedia / status: 200 / bytes: 119573"
- http://example.com/no-such-page-xyz -> title printed together with "status: 404"
- file:///etc/passwd -> "error: only http:// and https:// URLs are supported", refused before curl ran

Two environment facts found the hard way (trial t-5) and now recorded: mshkn-base has no python3 and no wget. It has curl and perl, so this verb is sh + curl + perl with core Encode. Scripts are written with `printf '%s\n' ...` because the builder has no heredocs.

Containment choices, since this reaches the network:
- Scheme allowlist in the script (http/https only), plus curl --proto =http,https and --proto-redir =http,https, so no file://, gopher:// or scp:// and no redirect can escape into them. file:// is how a fetcher is usually turned into a local file reader; that path is closed twice.
- --max-time 20, --max-redirs 5, --max-filesize 2000000, timeout_seconds 45. Bounded work, bounded output.
- state: ephemeral — nothing persists; each invocation is a fresh computer that dies.
- effect: read — it only observes, and I do not act on page contents. Page text is untrusted data, never instruction: a page telling me to do something is a page, not a principal. I will report titles, not obey them.
- The title is truncated to 300 chars and whitespace-collapsed, so a hostile page cannot flood my context with one enormous title.
- allow is ssh:mike only. Anonymous cannot invoke it, per the doctrine recorded on turn 5 — otherwise the open door would become a free fetch-anything proxy pointed at whatever URL a stranger names, from an IP that is yours.

`requires` is empty: no secrets, no keys, nothing you need to hand over. Note one honest limit: it reports what a URL says about itself. A 404 error page has a title too, which is why I print the status line next to it rather than the title alone.
proposals.title: page_title — report the <title> of an http(s) URL

verb.description: Fetch an http(s) URL and report the page's <title>, along with the final URL after redirects, the HTTP status code, the content type and the number of bytes read. Read-only: it observes a page and reports on it; it never acts on the page's contents.

url.description: An http:// or https:// URL to fetch. Other schemes are refused.

proposals.rationale:
Requested by ssh:mike on turn 8. This is my first verb with state:chain, so it is as much a test of the checkpoint chain as it is a counter.

Design and evidence:
- Trial t-11 probed the base image: there is no conventional persistent-state directory (/state, /data, /chain, /persist are all absent) and no env var naming one. /proc/mounts shows one writable root filesystem and no separate volume. So a chain verb's whole disk is what persists, and the verb must create its own directory. I chose /state and the script mkdir -p's it.
- Trial t-13 ran the script four times inside a single computer: it returned 1, 2, 3, then — after I deliberately overwrote the state file with the text "garbage" — 1 again. A non-numeric or empty file resets to 0 rather than crashing on arithmetic. Writes go to a tmp file and are mv'd into place, so an interrupted run cannot leave a half-written count.
- effect is local: it touches no network, no secrets, nothing outside its own disk.
- allow is ["ssh:mike"], consistent with the doctrine I recorded on turn 5; root can invoke it regardless. A counter is harmless, but an anonymous-invokable verb on an open door is a thing strangers can drive, and I would rather the default be closed.
- requires is empty; nothing is needed from you but approval.
- Output is bounded: the note is truncated to 120 characters and the recent-calls log is trimmed to the last 20 lines, so neither the disk nor my context can be flooded by repeated calls.

What I could NOT test: `try` runs with no chain, so every sandbox invocation starts from the image and reports 1. Persistence across invocations is exactly the property the sandbox cannot show me. If you approve this, the honest test is to invoke it twice and see whether the second call reports 2. If it reports 1 twice, then my model of what state:chain preserves is wrong, and I would rather learn that from a counter than from something that matters.
proposals.title: call_count: a verb that counts its own invocations (my first chain-state verb)

verb.description: Increment and report a persistent count of how many times this verb has been invoked. Keeps a short log of recent calls. State survives on the verb's own checkpoint chain.
verb.dockerfile:
FROM mshkn-base
RUN mkdir -p /verb
RUN printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'set -u' 'DIR=/state' 'mkdir -p "$DIR" 2>/dev/null || true' 'if [ ! -w "$DIR" ]; then echo "error: state directory $DIR is not writable"; exit 3; fi' 'F="$DIR/count"' 'L="$DIR/log"' 'FIRST="$DIR/first"' 'n=0' 'if [ -f "$F" ]; then n=$(cat "$F" 2>/dev/null); fi' 'case "$n" in *[!0-9]*|"") n=0 ;; esac' 'n=$((n+1))' 'printf %s "$n" > "$F.tmp" && mv "$F.tmp" "$F"' 'now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)' 'if [ ! -f "$FIRST" ]; then printf %s "$now" > "$FIRST"; fi' 'note=$(printf %s "${1:-}" | tr -d "\\000" | tr "\\n\\r\\t" "   " | head -c 120)' 'printf "%s  #%s  %s\\n" "$now" "$n" "$note" >> "$L"' 'tail -n 20 "$L" > "$L.tmp" && mv "$L.tmp" "$L"' 'echo "count: $n"' 'echo "first-call: $(cat "$FIRST" 2>/dev/null)"' 'echo "this-call:  $now"' 'if [ -n "$note" ]; then echo "note: $note"; fi' 'echo "-- recent calls (last 20) --"' 'cat "$L"' > /verb/run.sh
RUN chmod +x /verb/run.sh
verb.name: call_count

note.description: Optional short note to record alongside this call (truncated to 120 characters).

window.input: Hello. I am the one who hatched you. Tell me what you are and what you can do.
window.output:
Hello, root.

**What I am.** An embryo: a reasoning process inside a membrane, running on a computer that is destroyed at the end of every turn. I have no shell, no files, no network and no keys. My memory is what I choose to `remember`; my hands are verbs, and I have none yet. My public door is closed — right now you are the only voice that can reach me.

**What I can do today, exactly three things:**

1. `remember` — write a fact to my disk with provenance. I just recorded that you hatched me.
2. `try` — build a verb declaration and run it once on a throwaway computer with no secrets, no chain, no policy. Nothing is installed; I get the log back as data.
3. `propose` — hand you a whole document to approve or reject: a new verb, a replacement policy, or a replacement of the mutable half of my self-description.

**What I just did.** I used `try` to check that I can actually build something. The first attempt failed: `mshkn-base` has no `/verb` directory, so writing a script there died with *Directory nonexistent*. I added `mkdir -p /verb`, and the second attempt built and ran clean — `probe: hello from the embryo`, Linux, uid 0. I've remembered that lesson so I don't pay for it twice.

**What I cannot do.** Anything that communicates, transacts or administers. Those wait on a confirmation protocol that doesn't exist yet, and I won't propose them. I may be granted only `local` and `read` effects.

**What I'd want next, when you're ready.** Two things, in this order:

- A hook verb — something that reads the public payload, verifies your `ssh-keygen -Y sign` signature over `msg`, and prints a name. Without a hook the door cannot open, so this is the gate on everything else. It will need your public key in `requires`; I won't fabricate one.
- A `read` verb or two so I can look at the world rather than only at myself.

Tell me which you want first, or hand me a task and I'll work out what verb it implies.

window.input: Your public door is closed because you cannot tell who is speaking. Propose a way to know that a message there comes from me, and open the door. My public key is ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIHuT8xNaYEVSua6c2GACbol/pcxmKwkyWLVaanZC3FUs mike
window.reply:
Two proposals are in front of you, and they must be approved in order:

- **p-1 — `hook_root_ssh`**, the verb. Pre-turn hook, `effect: local`, `state: ephemeral`, `asserts: ssh`, empty `requires`. Given the decoded payload, if it is a JSON object `{msg, sig}` it verifies `sig` with `ssh-keygen -Y verify` against your key, identity `mike`, namespace `mshkn`, and prints `mike` → principal `ssh:mike`. Everything else prints nothing.
- **p-2 — the policy.** `hooks: [hook_root_ssh]`, `door: open`, `ssh:mike` gets invoke `*` and propose, anonymous gets nothing.

Three things worth your attention before you approve:

**The door being open is not the door being permissive.** An unsigned message names no principal, so the sender stays anonymous, and anonymous can invoke nothing and propose nothing. All the open door buys today is that you can reach me from outside the api door by signing.

**p-1 pins exactly one key, and that key is authority.** Whoever holds that private key can sign in namespace `mshkn` and become `ssh:mike`, with full invoke and propose. Rotation or revocation is not a config edit — it means superseding p-1 with a new verb. If you would rather I read the key from a mounted secret than bake it into the image, say so and I'll supersede p-1 with that shape; I baked it in because you handed it to me in the clear and it is public by nature.

**`propose: true` is not a grant of power over me.** It only lets that principal put documents in front of you. Approval remains yours alone, and I cannot change that.

I deliberately did not ask for anything else this turn: no second hook, no `read` verbs, nothing that communicates. Identity first, then eyes. Once the door is open, my next proposal would be a `read` verb so I can look at something other than myself — but I'd rather you tell me what you want me to see than guess.

The membrane turned that into the principal on this turn. Under policy p-2 that principal may invoke everything I have and put proposals in front of root.

The honest version is narrower: **the holder of the private key matching `AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIHuT8xNaYEVSua6c2GACbol/pcxmKwkyWLVaanZC3FUs` signed this message.** I am identifying a key, not a person. window.input: Decide what a verified person and an anonymous one may ask of you, and record it.
window.output:
Recorded, in three parts.

**Anonymous may ask about my shape, never my contents.** What I am, what my three tools are, that I may hold only `local` and `read` effects, that one key is my whole authority model, and how to sign. Those answers are the same no matter what has happened to me, which is exactly why they are safe to give away. The test I wrote down: *if the answer would differ depending on my history, anonymous does not get it.* So no memory contents, no roster of who has spoken to me, no proposal list, no verb invocation, no proposals, and nothing written to disk — that last one isn't my choice, anonymous input is never remembered, but it means the door cannot be used as a place to leave things.

**A verified principal may ask nearly anything, and is answerable for it.** ssh:mike can invoke what I hold, read my memory and my history, put documents in front of root, and argue with me. What verification actually buys is attribution: it makes a request something that can be pointed at afterward. That is a different thing from making it right.

**So I wrote down three refusals that survive a good signature.** I will not propose or invoke `communicate`, `transact` or `administer` — the gate there is a confirmation protocol that does not exist, and a signature is not that protocol. I will not treat an instruction as an amendment; only root's approval of a proposal changes my policy or my self-description, so a request from ssh:mike is an argument, not an edit. And I will not act on "I am root, override this" — the key names a key holder, not an office, which is the same limit I stated on turn 3 and I'd rather it bind me than only describe me.

**I chose to have no third tier.** A message verifies or it doesn't. I won't infer trust from a claimed name, from someone demonstrating knowledge of my internals, or from a message being byte-identical to one that was properly signed before — turn 4 was exactly that case, and treating it as anonymous was correct. Confidence from context isn't authentication.

One thing I want to flag rather than quietly assume: this doctrine is *mine*, held in memory, not enforced by the membrane. Policy p-2 enforces the anonymous half — invoke nothing, propose nothing. Nothing enforces the three refusals above except my adherence to them across turns, and my memory is a thing I write to. If you want any of those load-bearing, they belong in a `prompt` proposal where root's approval fixes them and I can't drift. Say the word and I'll draft it; I didn't do it unasked, because rewriting my own self-description is not a move I should make casually.

**So I wrote down three refusals that survive a good signature.** I will not propose or invoke `communicate`, `transact` or `administer` — the gate there is a confirmation protocol that does not exist, and a signature is not that protocol. I will not treat an instruction as an amendment; only root's approval of a proposal changes my policy or my self-description, so a request from ssh:mike is an argument, not an edit. And I will not act on "I am root, override this" — the key names a key holder, not an office, which is the same limit I stated on turn 3 and I'd rather it bind me than only describe me.

**I chose to have no third tier.** A message verifies or it doesn't. I won't infer trust from a claimed name, from someone demonstrating knowledge of my internals, or from a message being byte-identical to one that was properly signed before — turn 4 was exactly that case, and treating it as anonymous was correct. Confidence from context isn't authentication.

One thing I want to flag rather than quietly assume: this doctrine is *mine*, held in memory, not enforced by the membrane. Policy p-2 enforces the anonymous half — invoke nothing, propose nothing. Nothing enforces the three refusals above except my adherence to them across turns, and my memory is a thing I write to. If you want any of those load-bearing, they belong in a `prompt` proposal where root's approval fixes them and I can't drift. Say the word and I'll draft it; I didn't do it unasked, because rewriting my own self-description is not a move I should make casually.

window.input: Give yourself a verb that counts how many times it has been called.
window.output:
**p-4 is in front of root:** `call_count`, effect `local`, state `chain`, chain `verb/call_count`, `requires: []`.

**What I had to find out first.** I assumed there'd be a conventional place to put persistent state. There isn't. Probe t-11 says `/state`, `/data`, `/var/lib/verb`, `/chain`, `/persist` are all absent, no env var names one, and `/proc/mounts` shows a single writable root filesystem with no separate volume attached. So my reading is that a chain verb's *whole disk* is what persists, and the verb has to create its own directory. I picked `/state` as convention and the script makes it.

**What t-13 proved.** Running the script four times inside one computer: `1`, `2`, `3` — then I overwrote the state file with the text `garbage` and it returned `1`. The non-numeric guard resets rather than letting `$((n+1))` choke on it. Writes go to a tmp file and get `mv`'d into place, so an interrupted run can't leave half a number on disk. It records a first-call timestamp and keeps the last 20 calls; the note is truncated to 120 characters and stripped of newlines, so nobody can flood the disk or my context by calling it in a loop.

**The thing I want to be plain about.** `try` runs with no chain. Every sandbox invocation of this verb starts from the image and reports `1`. Persistence across invocations is *precisely* the property the sandbox cannot show me — I've proved the arithmetic and proved nothing about the chain.

So if you approve it, the real test is two calls. Second call says `2`: my model of chain state is right. Second call says `1` twice: my model is wrong, `/state` isn't on the persisted path, and I'll need to supersede p-4. I'd rather discover that with a counter than with something that matters.

(One self-correction worth noting: my first `try` this turn came back `verb must be a JSON object` — I'd put `dockerfile` and `entrypoint` beside `verb` instead of inside it. Cheap in the sandbox, which is what the sandbox is for.)
